unit.title: Support continuous improvement systems and processes

summary: This unit teaches you to lead small, tested improvements in a fabrication shop. You will use the PDCA cycle, measure with fair data and baselines, find root causes with Pareto charts, fishbone diagrams and the 5 whys, cut waste and organise the workplace with 5S, trial and mistake-proof changes without weakening safety or the WPS, involve your team, and monitor the results on run and control charts.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It teaches you to **support continuous improvement** in a fabrication shop: to find problems from facts, work out their real causes, try out better ways of working on a small scale, prove that they work, make them the standard way, and keep them going. You also learn to involve your team, so that improving the work becomes part of everyone's job.

Continuous improvement is not about big, expensive changes. It is about many **small, tested changes**: a jig that saves ten minutes a frame, a rule that keeps electrodes dry, a shelf that saves a walk to the store. Added up over hundreds of jobs, they make a shop safer, faster, cheaper and better. At Level 3 you are close enough to the work to see the problems, and senior enough to lead the fixes.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders, leading hands and supervisors in fabrication shops. The tools taught here work in any workshop.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the shop
rows: Say what it is, why small tested changes work, and what part each person plays.
Plan, Do, Check and Act on an improvement, step by step.
Choose clear measures, record a baseline, collect reliable data and work out the change.
Use check sheets, Pareto charts, fishbone diagrams and the 5 whys; tell a cause from a symptom.
Cut waste and organise the workplace
Spot the eight wastes, map a process, and use 5S.
Use ideas from the team, clients, inspection and near-miss reports; pick the best value; never weaken safety or the WPS; trial on a small scale; mistake-proof.
Involve people and make change stick
Encourage and answer ideas, deal with resistance, communicate change, and update procedures and training.
Plot results on run and control charts, act when results slip, and review procedures regularly.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on improvement basics, PDCA, data, problem analysis, waste, 5S, involving people, standards, safety, monitoring and mistake-proofing.

A **written paper** with short answers (terms and sums) and essays, for example PDCA, a Pareto analysis, a fishbone diagram, the wastes, jigs, a silent suggestion box, bringing in a new process, control charts, judging an unsafe idea and using complaints and reports.
**Two group practicals**: improving a repeat fabrication task with a jig through a full PDCA cycle; and inspecting defective samples, analysing the faults and presenting an improvement plan.

blocks.note: Learn the terms (kaizen, Pareto, poka-yoke, benchmarking, control chart, standard work, overproduction, transport, set in order) and practise the percentage and payback sums.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Continuous improvement** means always looking for, and making, small practical improvements to the way work is done, so that it becomes safer, better, faster or less wasteful, and then keeping the gains. The Japanese word **kaizen** ("change for the better") is often used for small, continuous improvements made by the people who do the work.

head: Small, tested changes
One sudden big change
rows: Each change can be tried, checked and undone if it does not work
If it goes wrong, everything is affected at once
The team learns as it goes
People may resist a change they did not help make
Gains add up over many jobs and months
Gains may never come if it fails

blocks.p: Big changes (a new machine, a new process) still have their place, but they too are best trialled and checked before they are rolled out.

A shop that is serious about improvement has a **system**: a regular way of finding problems, collecting ideas, choosing which to try, trialling them, keeping the ones that work and sharing the results.

flow: Find problems and ideas: the team, KPIs, inspection reports, complaints, near misses
Choose: the most benefit for the least cost and risk
Trial on a small scale, measuring before and after
Keep what works: write it into the procedure and train everyone
Show the results and thank the people involved
Review regularly, and look for the next improvement

head: Person
Part in the improvement system
rows: Sets the direction, provides time and money, approves bigger changes, recognises good work
Leads improvement in the team: collects and answers ideas, organises trials, checks results, updates procedures
Spots problems, gathers data, trials changes, reports results, coaches others in the new method
Follows the standard method, suggests ideas, reports problems and near misses
Provides inspection data; checks that changes keep the quality the job needs

blocks.p: The best sign that improvement has become part of a shop's culture is that **people spot and fix problems as part of their daily work**, without waiting to be told. Problems are seen as chances to improve, not as reasons to blame someone.

blocks.note: Improvement never means weakening safety, the welding procedure specification (WPS), the code the job must meet or the client's requirements. An idea that saves time by removing a safety control or a quality step is not an improvement.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **PDCA** (Plan, Do, Check, Act) gives the steps for every improvement. When one cycle finishes, the next begins.

head: Step
What you do
Questions to ask
rows: Pick the problem; measure the present situation (the baseline); find the causes; set a target; plan a change and how to measure it
What is the problem? How big is it now? What causes it? What will we try? How will we know it worked?
Try the change on a small scale (a few frames, one bay, one shift); train the people involved; record the results
Did we do what we planned? What happened?
Compare the results with the baseline and the target; if it did not work, find out why
Did it improve things? Were there side effects?
If it works, make it the standard: update the procedure, train everyone, keep checking. If not, learn from it and plan again
How do we keep the gain? What next?

blocks.h: A worked example: dross on plasma-cut plates

head: Step
What the team did
rows: Grinding dross off plasma-cut bracket plates took 6 minutes a plate (timed on 20 plates). A fishbone pointed to worn nozzles and electrodes, wrong cutting speed and wet compressed air. Target: 2 minutes a plate. Change: a start-up checklist (consumables, air dryer, cut chart settings).
The checklist was used on one table for one week; the operators were shown how; grinding times were recorded on 20 plates.
Grinding fell to 2.5 minutes a plate: (6 − 2.5) ÷ 6 × 100 = about 58% less. Edge quality was also better. The target was not quite met: worn nozzles were still being used too long.
The checklist went into the cutting procedure, with a nozzle-change rule; all operators were trained; times are checked monthly. The next cycle tackles the remaining half-minute.

blocks.note: Do not skip Plan and jump to a solution. Without a baseline you cannot prove the change worked, and without the cause you may fix the wrong thing.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A good measure shows clearly whether the problem is getting better. Use **rates**, not just counts, when the amount of work changes from week to week: "weld repairs per 100 welds inspected" is fairer than "number of repairs", because a busy week has more welds and so more chances for repairs.

head: Measure
How it is worked out
rows: Items passing inspection with no rework ÷ items inspected × 100
Minutes of fit-up (or welding, or grinding) per frame
Hours spent on rework per month, or per tonne of steel
J$ of rework, scrap or consumables per job

blocks.p: A measure used to track how well a process is doing is a **key performance indicator (KPI)**.
The **baseline** is the measure **before** the change, recorded long enough to be fair (for example a month of repairs, or 20 frames timed). Without it, nobody can show whether the change helped.

ul: Everyone measures the **same way**: agree the method (what counts as a repair, where a frame's diagonal is measured from).
Use **accurate tools**: check gauges, tapes and timers, and calibrate them.
If two people measure the same weld and get different answers, stop, agree the method and check the gauges before the data is used.
Record data as it happens, on a **check sheet** (a simple tally sheet), not from memory.

head: Question
Working
Answer
rows: 400 welds radiographed; 28 needed repair. Repair rate?
180 frames inspected; 171 passed first time. First-time pass rate?
Fit-up fell from 40 to 25 minutes a frame. Percentage saving?
Rework fell from 80 to 52 hours a month. Percentage removed?
A clamp saves 3 minutes a frame; 120 frames a month. Hours saved?
A jig costs J$72,000 and saves J$8,000 a month. Payback?

blocks.note: For a percentage change, always divide by the **old** (before) figure.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **symptom** is what you see: porous welds, frames out of square, rework hours. The **root cause** is why it happens: damp electrodes, no square at the bay. Grinding out and re-welding porous welds every week fixes the welds but not the problem, so the porosity keeps coming back. Improvement aims at root causes.

A **Pareto chart** is a bar chart of causes in order from most to least frequent, often with a line for the running total. It usually shows that a few causes make up most of the problem (often called the 80/20 rule), so the team knows where to start.
Here the top two faults, distortion and undercut, are 22 + 13 = 35 of the 50, which is 70% of the problem. The team starts with distortion, the biggest single cause.

The problem goes at the "head" of the fish. The main "bones" are groups of possible causes, often **people, method, machine, materials, measurement and environment**. The team fills in likely causes under each, from experience and data.

head: Bone
Possible causes of distortion on balcony rails
rows: Welders new to the job; not trained in the weld sequence
Long runs welded from one end; no tacking order; parts not clamped
Current set too high; worn torch giving an unsteady arc
Thin tube; steel already bent when delivered
Rails checked only after all welding, when it is too late
Uneven bench; rails stacked hot on top of each other

head: Question
Answer
rows: Why did the rail fail the straightness check?
The balusters were welded all along one side first.
There is no written weld sequence for rails.
The job was set up quickly and nobody wrote one.
New jobs have no step for setting a weld sequence: **root cause**. Action: add a weld-sequence sheet to the new-job set-up.

blocks.p: Keep asking "why?" until you reach something the team can fix that stops the problem coming back. It may take fewer or more than five.

ul: **Stratify** the data: split it by machine, welder, shift, bay, position, material batch or time of day. If most defects come from one MIG set, check that set first (gas, liner, settings, earth connection).
Test likely causes one at a time, so you know which change made the difference.
Base decisions on data, not on who shouts loudest or who is easiest to blame.

blocks.p: **Waste** is anything that uses time, money, space or effort without adding value for the client. Value is added only when the work changes the product in a way the client wants and will pay for: cutting, fitting, welding, finishing to the drawing. The eight wastes are often remembered as **TIMWOODS**.

head: Waste
What it is
Fabrication example
A possible fix
rows: Moving materials or parts more than needed
Plate cut at one end of the shop, drilled at the far end, then carried back to weld
Re-lay the shop so the steps sit in order
Stock or work-in-progress beyond what is needed
Two years' supply of a rarely used electrode
Order to need; set maximum stock
People moving more than the work needs
Welders walking to the store for every disc and tip
Keep common consumables at each bay
Frames waiting days for the painter or the crane
Plan crane and painter time; schedule the next step
Making more than ordered, or long before it is needed
Cutting 30 gate panels when 5 are ordered
Make to orders and the programme
Doing more than the client needs
Grinding welds smooth that will be hidden behind cladding
Work that must be repaired or scrapped
Porous welds ground out and rewelded
Not using people's skills and ideas
A 6G pipe welder kept sweeping and carrying
Match tasks to skills; ask for ideas

blocks.p: A **process map** shows every step a job goes through, in order, for example from cutting to dispatch. Mark each step as **value-adding** (cut, fit, weld, finish) or **not** (move, wait, store, re-check). If a gate goes through 9 steps and only 4 add value, the team looks at removing or shortening the other 5. Some non-value steps, such as inspection, are still needed, but can often be made quicker.
A **spaghetti diagram** (a plan of the shop with a line drawn wherever a part or person travels) shows transport and motion waste clearly.

head: Step
Japanese word
What it means in a welding bay
rows: Remove everything not needed in the bay: broken chairs, old jigs, scrap
A place for everything and everything in its place: shadow boards, labelled hooks for leads, marked spots for bottles and bins
Clean the bay every shift, and check leads, torches and guards for damage while cleaning
Write down and photograph how the bay should look; the same layout in every bay
Keep it up: short daily checks, a weekly audit score on the board, leaders setting the example

blocks.note: 5S fails when it is a one-off clean-up. Two months later the bays are messy again. Short daily checks and a weekly audit score that everyone can see keep it going.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **visual management board** in the workshop shows the team's key measures, problems and actions for all to see, updated each week (often at a short stand-up meeting). Seeing progress keeps people interested, and problems cannot hide.

head: Source
Example
What it can lead to
rows: A welder suggests a hinge jig
Gates arrive with chipped paint at the hinges
A Pareto and fishbone; an electrode oven and a store rule
A plate slipped from a lifting clamp
Checked clamps, training and lifting method before someone is hurt
Rework hours rising on one product
The painter, inspector and delivery driver each see a different part of the process
Ideas the welders would never see
Comparing the shop's repair rate with the best shops
A clear target and ideas from others

blocks.p: Give priority to the idea with the **most benefit for the least cost and risk**. A simple way is to sort ideas into four boxes: high benefit and low effort (do first), high benefit and high effort (plan carefully), low benefit and low effort (do when convenient), low benefit and high effort (drop).

**Payback period = cost ÷ saving per month.** A J$15,000 jig that saves 10 hours a month at J$1,500 an hour (J$15,000 a month) pays for itself in about 1 month. A J$2.5 million machine may be worth it, but needs a full case.

ul: Judge every idea first against **safety, quality, the WPS, the code and the client's standard**, and only then against cost and time.
A change to a welding method on coded work needs a **qualified WPS** and **approved welders** before it is used on that job.
Do not remove safety controls (fire watch, fume extraction, guards, permits) to save time or money.
If an idea fails these tests, say no, explain why, and look for another way to get the benefit.

blocks.p: **Poka-yoke** is a Japanese term for a simple device or design that makes a mistake impossible, or shows it at once. A jig that a bracket fits only the right way round, a pin that stops a part being loaded backwards, a gauge that only fits a correct gap, a checklist that must be ticked before the machine starts.

A **jig** holds parts in the right place while they are tacked and welded. Every part goes against the same stops, so frames come out the same size and square: less measuring, less rework, faster fit-up, and less-experienced workers can fit up accurately under supervision. A jig can also hold the work in an easier, safer welding position. Jigs wear and get knocked, so they are checked for accuracy at set intervals.

flow: Record the baseline: the same measures, the old way, on enough items
Make the change on a small scale: a few frames, one bay or one shift
Keep everything else the same (the same welders, materials and job), so the change is the only difference
Record the same measures in the same way
Compare, and look for side effects such as new faults or safety problems
Decide: keep it, change it and trial again, or drop it

blocks.p: Trialling on a few frames first means problems are found while little is at risk. If the trial is done only by the best welders, part of the gain may come from their skill, not the change: include ordinary welders too.

head: Action
Owner (one person)
By when
How we will measure it
rows: Make and check the hinge jig

blocks.p: Each action has **one named person** who will see it done by a date, even if others help.

sections.title: Involving people and making change stick

blocks.p: A jig designed in the office without asking the welders may not suit how the work is really done. The people who do the job know its problems best, and they support changes they helped to make.

A suggestion box can go silent for months. Common reasons: past ideas got no answer, people fear being laughed at or blamed, they think improvement is the managers' job, some find writing difficult, and nobody has time set aside.

ul: Answer every idea, quickly (for example within a week), even when the answer is no, with the reason.
Make it easy: ideas spoken at the weekly toolbox meeting, written on a board, or told to the team leader, not only written in a box.
Trial good ideas **with** the person who suggested them, and show the results on the board.
Give thanks and credit in front of the team.
Set a small, clear problem each month (for example cutting grinding time) and ask for ideas on it.
When an idea is tried and does not work, thank the person, share what was learned, and invite more ideas.

blocks.p: People resist change when they do not see why it is needed, fear it will make their job harder, were not asked, or find the new way awkward. If the night shift ignores a new record sheet, first **find out why**: perhaps it takes too long, is unclear, or nobody explained it. Then fix the reason.

flow: Explain why the change is being made, and show the trial results
Make sure everything is ready: equipment, materials, stock, and a qualified WPS and approved welders where the work is coded
Demonstrate the new method, and let people practise
Update the written procedure or work instruction, and remove the old one
Train everyone who does the job, and record the training
Watch closely in the first weeks, measure the results and fix problems quickly
Review the results with the team after a set time

blocks.p: **Standard work** is the fixed, agreed best way of doing a job that everyone follows, written down with photos or sketches. It keeps the gain, makes training easier, and gives the base for the next improvement. Procedures are still **reviewed from time to time**, even when they seem to work, because work, materials, machines and people change.
When a method works on one product, look at whether it can be used on others. A method that halves rework on gates may also work on grilles and railings.

A **run chart** plots a measure over time (for example weld repairs per 100 welds each week) with the weeks along the bottom. It shows trends far better than single numbers. Mark on it when the change was made, and put it on the board where everyone can see it.

A **control chart**, used in statistical process control, is a run chart with a centre line (the average) and an **upper** and a **lower control limit** worked out from the data. Points scattered between the limits are normal variation. Common signs that something has changed:

ul: a point outside a limit;
a long run of points (often seven or more) all on one side of the centre line;
a steady trend of points going up or down.

blocks.p: When you see a sign, find out **what changed** at that time: a new welder, a new batch of wire, a worn jig, an oven left off, the method not being followed.

ul: Do not just blame people. Look for what has changed.
Fix the cause, retrain where needed, and keep watching the chart.
Check that tools and jigs are still accurate.
Set a review date to decide whether more improvement is needed.

blocks.p: Faults cost more the later they are found. A weld repair found in the shop costs grinding, welding and inspection time. The same repair found at the client's site adds travel, access equipment, delay to the client and lost goodwill, and maybe the next contract. That is why prevention (training, dry electrodes, jigs, checks at fit-up) pays.

head: Kind of cost
Example
rows: Site repairs, travel, claims, lost goodwill

blocks.p: Report improvements to management with the before-and-after figures, the cost and the saving, and the people who made it happen. Small savings across many jobs add up, and showing them keeps support for the next improvement.

blocks.note: Many Jamaican shops are open-sided and close to the sea. When results change, think about the weather and the season too: sea breezes blow away shielding gas, the rainy seasons bring damp electrodes and wet steel, and heat affects people and machines. Stratify your data by season and bay to see it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and work on it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain continuous improvement and kaizen, and why small tested changes are safer than one big change.
I can describe a shop's improvement system and the part each person plays.
I can explain each step of PDCA with a workshop example.
I can choose a fair measure, record a baseline and collect reliable data.
I can work out rates, percentage changes, hours saved and payback periods.
I can tell a symptom from a root cause.
I can draw a Pareto chart and work out the share of the top causes.
I can draw a fishbone diagram and use the 5 whys.
I can name the eight wastes, with a fabrication example and a fix for each.
I can map a process and pick out the steps that add value.
I can explain and lead the five steps of 5S, and keep them going.
I can use complaints, inspection reports, near misses and benchmarking as sources of improvement.
I can choose the best-value improvement and judge ideas against safety, quality and the WPS first.
I can explain mistake-proofing and how a jig improves quality and speed.
I can run a fair small-scale trial and write an action plan with owners and dates.
I can encourage ideas, answer them and deal with resistance.
I can bring in a change so that it is used correctly and kept up.
I can read a run chart and a control chart and act when results slip.

terms: 5 whys
Asking "why?" again and again until the root cause is found
5S
Sort, set in order, shine, standardise, sustain: a method for organising the workplace
Baseline
The measure of a process before a change, used to judge the change
Benchmarking
Comparing your results with the best shops to find where to improve
Check sheet
A simple tally sheet for recording data as it happens
Continuous improvement
Always making small, tested improvements to the way work is done
Control chart
A chart that plots a measure over time between an upper and a lower limit line
Fishbone diagram
A cause-and-effect diagram with the problem at the head and groups of causes as bones
Jig
A device that holds parts in the right place for fit-up and welding
Kaizen
Japanese for "change for the better": small, continuous improvements by the people who do the work
KPI
Key performance indicator: a measure used to track how well a process is doing
Overproduction
Making more than the client ordered, or making it long before it is needed
Over-processing
Doing more work on a product than the client needs
Pareto chart
A bar chart of causes from most to least frequent, often with a running-total line
Payback period
How long the savings from a change take to cover its cost
PDCA
Plan, Do, Check, Act: the improvement cycle
Poka-yoke
A simple device or design that makes a mistake impossible; mistake-proofing
Process map
A diagram of every step a job goes through, in order
Root cause
The underlying reason a problem happens, which stops it coming back when fixed
Run chart
A chart of a measure plotted over time
Standard work
The fixed, agreed best way of doing a job that everyone follows
Symptom
The visible sign of a problem, not its cause
Transport
The waste of moving materials or parts more than the job needs
Visual management board
A board in the workshop showing the team's measures, problems and actions
Waste
Anything that uses time, money, space or effort without adding value for the client

c1.title: Balcony rail defects in Discovery Bay
c1.text: A shop in Discovery Bay, St Ann, makes steel balcony rails for villas with MIG welding. Over two months the inspector logged 80 defects: porosity 36, distortion 18, undercut 14, spatter left on 6 and wrong length 6. Most of the porosity is on welds made in the bay next to the sea-facing roller door, on windy afternoons. The team leader, Tameka, has asked the team to tackle the problem.

c2.title: A walk through a gate shop in Harbour View
c2.text: In a gate shop in Harbour View, Kingston, welders walk about 40 m to the store several times a day for discs, wire and contact tips. The grinders and clamps for four bays are kept in one shared box. The shop cuts gate panels 30 at a time, although orders come in for 4 to 6 gates a week. Bay 2 holds broken chairs and two old jigs that nobody uses. A process map of one gate shows 9 steps from cutting to dispatch.

c3.title: A drawbar jig trial in Chapelton
c3.text: At a shop in Chapelton, Clarendon, fitting up a trailer drawbar frame took 30 minutes on average, and 3 of the last 20 frames were out of square. The team made a fit-up jig for J$54,000 and trialled it on 10 frames, all made by the shop's two most experienced welders: fit-up took 18 minutes on average and none was out of square. Labour costs J$1,800 an hour, and the shop makes 100 frames a month.

c4.title: The ideas board in Highgate
c4.text: A fabrication shop in Highgate, St Mary, started an ideas board three months ago. Fourteen ideas have gone up, and six have had no reply after more than a month. Kemoy has suggested switching off the fume extraction when welders are "only tacking", to save electricity. Other ideas include: a J$2.5 million CNC plasma table; labelled hooks for welding leads, J$6,000, saving about 1 labour hour a month; a J$15,000 hinge jig, saving about 10 labour hours a month; and re-roofing the store, J$900,000. Labour costs J$1,500 an hour.

c5.title: Watching repair rates in Junction
c5.text: A shop in Junction, St Elizabeth, plots weekly weld repairs per 100 welds on a chart in the workshop. Before an electrode oven was installed, repairs averaged 9.6 per 100 welds; in the eight weeks after, they averaged 4.8. The team then drew control limits around the new level: upper limit 7, lower limit 2. In week 14 the point jumps to 9. The supervisor finds that the oven was switched off over a long holiday weekend.

questions.q: What share of all the defects do the top two causes make up?
questions.why: In Pareto order the top two are porosity (36) and distortion (18): 36 + 18 = 54 defects, and 54 ÷ 80 × 100 = 67.5%. Working on these two first tackles two-thirds of the problem.

questions.q: Which change should Tameka's team trial first for the porosity?
o: Retrain every welder in the shop on their MIG technique
Change to a different make of MIG wire in all four bays
Turn the gas flow up as high as the regulator will go
Screen that bay from the wind and compare porosity
questions.why: The data points to one bay on windy afternoons, which suggests draughts blowing the shielding gas away. Testing that one likely cause first, and measuring the result, is better than changing everything at once.

questions.q: On the team's fishbone diagram, under which main bone does "nozzle blocked with spatter" belong?
o: Machine
Materials
Method
Environment
questions.why: The nozzle is part of the welding equipment, so it goes under Machine. Draughts would go under Environment, and dirty plate under Materials.

questions.q: After the change, porosity fell from 12 to 4 per 100 welds. What is the percentage reduction?
o: About 33%
About 67%
questions.why: (12 − 4) ÷ 12 × 100 = about 67%. Always divide by the old figure; dividing by the new one gives the wrong answer of 200%, and 8 is the drop in welds, not a percentage.

questions.q: Cutting gate panels 30 at a time when only 4 to 6 gates are ordered each week is mainly which kind of waste?
o: Over-processing
Waiting
Transport
Overproduction
questions.why: Making more than is ordered, or long before it is needed, is overproduction. It ties up steel, money and floor space, and stored panels can rust or be damaged.

questions.q: Which change would best cut the waste of the welders' walks to the store?
o: Keep a small, labelled stock of common items at each bay
Fetch a whole month's supply at once and stack it in the bays
Lock the store at set times so that fewer trips are made
Have one welder fetch everyone's items at the start of the day
questions.why: The walking is motion waste. A small, labelled stock of discs, wire and tips at each bay, topped up daily, removes most trips without creating a big pile of stock (inventory waste).

questions.q: Cleaning bay 2 at the end of every shift, and checking leads and torches for damage while cleaning, is which 5S step?
o: Sort
Standardise
Shine
Sustain
questions.why: Shine means cleaning the workplace and using the cleaning to inspect equipment. Removing the broken chairs and old jigs would be Sort.

questions.q: Which step on the gate's process map adds value?
o: Carrying panels from the saw to the welding bay
Welding the hinges onto the gate frame
Storing cut panels until an order comes in
Measuring each panel again before welding
questions.why: Value is added only when the product is changed in a way the client wants and pays for. Moving, storing and re-checking do not change the gate, so the team looks at cutting or shortening them.

questions.q: How long will the jig take to pay for itself?
o: About 2.5 months
About 30 months
About 6 months
About 1.5 months
questions.why: 12 minutes saved × 100 frames = 1,200 minutes = 20 hours a month. 20 × J$1,800 = J$36,000 a month, and 54,000 ÷ 36,000 = 1.5 months.

questions.q: Which result from the trial is the strongest evidence that the jig works?
o: Faster fit-up and no frames out of square across all 10
The two welders said they much preferred using the new jig
The jig looks very solid and was made from good heavy steel
The very first frame in the jig went faster than usual
questions.why: Measured results on the same measures as the baseline, over several frames, are evidence. Opinions, looks and a single frame are not.

questions.q: Why might the trial make the jig look better than it really is?
o: Ten frames are far too many items for a fair trial
The gain may come partly from the welders' skill
A jig made in the shop can never be truly accurate
The baseline frames were measured with a tape
questions.why: In a fair trial the change is the only difference. If only the best welders used the jig, part of the improvement may be their skill, so ordinary welders should be included before the jig is made standard.

questions.q: How should the team leader answer Kemoy's idea about the fume extraction?
o: Try it for a month and see whether anyone feels unwell
Agree, as tacking makes far less fume than full welding
Ignore it, since safety matters are for managers alone
Say no, explain the fume risk, and ask for other ideas
questions.why: Fume extraction is a safety control and is not removed to save money. Thanking Kemoy, explaining why and pointing him to other savings, such as switching off idle machines, keeps him offering ideas.

questions.q: What is the main risk of leaving six ideas unanswered for over a month?
o: People stop offering ideas, thinking nobody listens
The board fills up and a bigger one has to be bought
The owner may be blamed for too many changes at once
The unanswered ideas will all be tried at the same time
questions.why: When ideas get no reply, people decide the scheme is for show and stop contributing. Every idea needs a quick answer, even when the answer is no.

questions.q: Which idea gives the most benefit for the least cost and risk?
o: The labelled hooks
The CNC plasma table
The hinge jig
Re-roofing the store
questions.why: The hinge jig saves 10 hours × J$1,500 = J$15,000 a month, so it pays for itself in about a month. The hooks save only about J$1,500 a month (4 months' payback), and the big items need a full case.

questions.q: By what percentage did the oven reduce the repair rate?
questions.why: (9.6 − 4.8) ÷ 9.6 × 100 = 50%. The rate halved. Dividing by the new figure would give 100%, which is wrong.

questions.q: What should the supervisor do after finding why week 14 jumped?
o: Add an oven check to the daily start-up list
Warn all the welders that repairs must come down
Redraw the limits so a 9 falls inside them
Leave week 14 off the chart as a one-off
questions.why: A point above the upper limit shows something changed, and the cause is known. Fixing it so it cannot happen again, for example a start-up check, keeps the gain; then keep plotting.

questions.q: Why is "repairs per 100 welds" a better measure for this chart than the number of repairs?
o: It makes the chart much easier to draw by hand
The number of welds changes from week to week
Clients always ask for figures given in hundreds
It hides the weeks that had very few repairs
questions.why: A busy week has more welds and so more chances for repairs. A rate per 100 welds compares weeks fairly, so the chart shows real change, not just changes in workload.

questions.q: A team tries a new weld sequence on six railings and records the distortion on each. Which PDCA step is this?
o: Plan
Do
Check
Act
questions.why: Do means carrying out the change on a small scale and recording the results. Comparing the results with the baseline comes next, in Check.

questions.q: A Level 3 welder with a 6G pipe qualification spends most days sweeping and carrying steel. Which waste is this?
o: Over-processing
Unused skills
Transport
Waiting
questions.why: Not using people's skills and ideas is the eighth waste. The shop is paying for skills it is not using, and the welder's ideas and talent are lost to the work.

questions.q: A shop keeps finding porosity in its bracket welds. Which of these is a root cause rather than a symptom?
o: Porosity found in the bracket welds
Hours spent grinding out and rewelding
Rising repair costs on the monthly report
No rule for storing opened electrodes
questions.why: The porosity, the rework hours and the costs are what you see. Having no rule for keeping opened electrodes dry is why it happens, and fixing it stops the porosity coming back.
